matrix-modeling-s1.title: A two-station bike share
matrix-modeling-s1.text: A bike-share system has $500$ bikes. Today $400$ are at station A and $100$ at station B. The diagram shows the chance that a bike moves or stays each day.

matrix-modeling-s2.title: Sunny and rainy days
matrix-modeling-s2.text: In one town, tomorrow's weather depends only on today's. Today is rainy.

table.caption: Chance of tomorrow's weather (rows) given today's weather (columns)

items.q: Which transition matrix, with "from" columns (A, B) and "to" rows (A, B), models one day?

why.correct: Column 1 is a bike at A: stays $0.8$, goes to B $0.2$. Column 2 is a bike at B: goes to A $0.3$, stays $0.7$. Each column adds up to $1$.
options: This puts "from" in the rows; its columns add up to $1.1$ and $0.9$.
The chances for B are reversed: a bike at B stays with chance $0.7$.
The stay and move chances are swapped.

items.q: How many bikes are expected at station A after one day?

mistakes.why: That uses rows as "from": $0.8(400) + 0.2(100)$. Bikes arriving at A from B come with chance $0.3$: $0.8(400) + 0.3(100)$.
$320$ bikes stay at A, but $0.3(100) = 30$ more arrive from B.

items.q: How many bikes are expected at station A after two days?

mistakes.why: That is after one day. Multiply by $T$ again.
$300$ is the long-run number; after two days the count is still on its way there.

why.correct: $\mathbf{x}_1 = \left[ \begin{matrix} 350 \\ 150 \end{matrix} \right]$, so after two days A has $0.8(350) + 0.3(150) = 280 + 45 = 325$ bikes.

items.q: In the long run, how many bikes are expected at station A?

mistakes.why: The stations do not split evenly. Balance the flows: $0.2a = 0.3b$ with $a + b = 500$.
The count moves away from the start: $350$, $325$, ... Solve $0.2a = 0.3b$, $a + b = 500$.

items.q: Today's state is $\left[ \begin{matrix} 400 \\ 100 \end{matrix} \right]$. Which calculation gives the expected state yesterday?

options: A negative matrix gives negative bike counts; undoing a step needs the inverse.

items.q: What is the chance that it is sunny two days from today?

mistakes.why: $0.5$ is the chance for tomorrow. Multiply by the matrix twice.
$0.9$ is the chance of sun after a sunny day; today is rainy.

items.q: What is the chance that it is sunny five days from today? Give your answer correct to three decimal places.

mistakes.why: That starts from a sunny day. Today is rainy: use $T^5$ times the vector $(0, 1)$.
That is the long-run chance. After five days the chance is still slightly below it.

why.correct: Enter $T$ in the calculator and compute $T^5\left[ \begin{matrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{matrix} \right]$: the first entry is $0.8248$.

items.q: In the long run, what share of days are sunny? Give your answer correct to three decimal places.

mistakes.why: $0.9$ is the chance of sun after a sunny day. Solve $0.1s = 0.5(1 - s)$ for the steady share.
That is the chance two days out. Find the steady state, or compute $T^n$ for large $n$.

why.correct: At a steady state the flows balance: $0.1s = 0.5(1 - s)$, so $0.6s = 0.5$ and $s = \frac{5}{6} \approx 0.833$. A calculator check: $T^{30}$ has both columns close to $(0.833, 0.167)$.

items.q: Which expression gives the weather state five days from today?

why.correct: Each day multiplies by $T$, so five days multiply by $T^5$. Today is rainy: the vector $(0, 1)$.
options: $5T$ multiplies each chance by $5$; chances above $1$ make no sense.
The state lists chances that add up to $1$, not a count of days.
This starts from a sunny day.

items.q: Why does each column of a transition matrix (with "from" columns) add up to 1?
options: Everything in a state ends the step in some state
Each row lists the states something can come from
The state vector has two entries

why.correct: A column lists the chances for one starting state across every possible ending state, and something must end somewhere.
options: The chances for one starting state cover every outcome.
Rows collect arrivals; their sums can be anything.
Columns adding up to 1 does not make a matrix invertible.
The number of entries does not set the sum.

items.q: Which could be a transition matrix with "from" columns?

why.correct: Entries between $0$ and $1$, and each column adds up to $1$: $0.6 + 0.4$ and $0.1 + 0.9$.
options: Valid chances, columns add up to $1$.
Its columns add up to $1.2$ and $0.8$.

items.q: For $T = \left[ \begin{matrix} 0.9 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.8 \end{matrix} \right]$, what share is in the first state at the steady state?

mistakes.why: That is the second state. Balance $0.1a = 0.2b$: $a = 2b$, so $a = \frac{2}{3}$.
$0.9$ is a one-step chance, not the long-run share.

items.q: With $T = \left[ \begin{matrix} 0.8 & 0.3 \\ 0.2 & 0.7 \end{matrix} \right]$, a share $p$ of the bikes start at A and $1 - p$ at B. Write the share at A after one day.

mistakes.why: Bikes arrive at A from B with chance $0.3$ (row 1, column 2), not $0.2$.
Add the bikes arriving from B: $0.3(1 - p)$.

items.q: Why does $T^{-1}$ give the state one step earlier?
options: $T^{-1}$ has the same columns as $T$ in reverse order
Each column of $T^{-1}$ adds up to $-1$
$T^{-1}$ is $T$ with each chance replaced by its reciprocal

why.correct: One step forward from $\mathbf{y}$ gives $\mathbf{x}$: $T\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x}$. The inverse undoes $T$, so $\mathbf{y} = T^{-1}\mathbf{x}$.
options: Swapping columns is a different matrix, not the inverse.
Column sums are not the reason; for an invertible transition matrix the columns of $T^{-1}$ add up to $1$, not $-1$.
Reciprocals of entries do not undo matrix multiplication.

items.q: The 500 bikes start with more at A, say 450 at A and 50 at B, instead of 400 and 100. Predict each change.

variables.name: The number of bikes at A after one day
variables.why: $0.8(450) + 0.3(50) = 375$, more than $350$: more bikes start where most stay.

variables.name: The long-run number at A
variables.why: The steady state comes from $T$ and the total, $500$: still $300$.

why.correct: The start changes the next few days, not where the system settles.

items.q: Put the steps for predicting the state two steps ahead in order.
options: Write the transition matrix $T$ with "from" columns
Check that each column of $T$ adds up to $1$
Compute $\mathbf{x}_1 = T\mathbf{x}_0$ from the current state $\mathbf{x}_0$

why.correct: Set up $T$ and check it, then step forward twice (or compute $T^2\mathbf{x}_0$ at once).
